name: Alpine tundra
notes: High-mountain zone above treeline (Rockies, Alps, Himalaya, Andes): fellfield, scree and cushion communities with prostrate willows, cushion plants, sedges and lichens. Drawn on Rocky Mountains, Alps and Himalaya.

shrub.name: Alpine azalea
shrub.source: Kalmia procumbens (Loiseleuria), circumpolar Arctic-alpine wind-swept ridges, prostrate evergreen mat with pink flowers

traits.native_range: Kalmia procumbens (Loiseleuria), circumpolar Arctic-alpine wind-swept ridges, prostrate evergreen mat with pink flowers
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are minute, with tiny, thick, dark-green, rolled-edged leaves in opposite pairs on wiry reddish stems. Very slow, they creep and branch into a dense, flat, trailing evergreen mat a few cm high that hugs wind-swept rock and gravel, dotted with small pink cup-bells in early summer.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Kalmia procumbens, formerly Loiseleuria: rarely over 10 cm, clusters of 2-5 rose-pink bell-shaped flowers late spring and summer, alpine and arctic heaths and bogs); growth and ages estimated from arctic-alpine dwarf-shrub mats.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (2-5 rose-pink bells per cluster); small reddish capsules splitting in late summer and persisting are typical of the species; pollinators (flies, bumblebees, selfing), timings and counts estimated.

shrub.name: Net-leaved willow
shrub.source: Salix reticulata, circumpolar Arctic-alpine calcareous ground, prostrate rounded net-veined leaves

traits.native_range: Salix reticulata, circumpolar Arctic-alpine calcareous ground, prostrate rounded net-veined leaves
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

shrub.silhouette: ground-hugging mat of round net-veined leaves

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling minute with two round cotyledons; first leaves small, round and dark green. Stems creep on or just under the ground and root, forming a flat mat; each short shoot carries 2-4 round, leathery leaves with a deeply sunken net of veins (whitish below) and, later, slender long-stalked catkins standing upright above the mat.
growth.source: Wikipedia/Flora of N America Salix reticulata (to 8 cm tall, exposed stems to 20 cm, mats 30 cm+ broad; slender yellow catkins tipped pink in spring); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (fast germination); spread rate, first seed and lifespan estimated for an arctic-alpine dwarf shrub

fruiting.source: Wikipedia/Flora of N America Salix reticulata (slender long-stalked catkins after the leaves, yellow tipped pink, females reddish; hairy capsules); insect plus wind pollination as in other arctic willows; ripening, set and crop estimated

shrub.name: Rocky Mountain snow willow

growth.juvenile_note: Willow seed germinates within days on wet gravel. The seedling has two tiny round cotyledons, then small dark leaves; its stems creep along and under the ground and root, building over decades a flat mat only a few centimetres high of small, glossy, net-veined leaves, with short reddish catkins standing just above it after the leaves come out.
growth.source: Flora of North America Salix nivalis (dwarf, trailing, to 5 cm; leaves elliptic to obovate, 0.4-2 cm, glossy, net-veined, glaucous beneath; catkins small, on leafy shoots); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Salix (seed germinates within days). Spread, first seed and age estimated.

shrub.source: Salix nivalis Hook., snow willow (accepted in Kew POWO; often treated as Salix reticulata subsp. nivalis): western Canada to the western and west-central USA, alpine fellfield, turf and snowbeds, mostly on calcareous ground; a trailing dwarf willow to 5 cm with small glossy net-veined leaves. Kew POWO; Flora of North America.

traits.native_range: Rocky Mountain and Cascade alpine tundra
traits.trunk: creeping stems on and under the ground
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: thin red-brown to grey-brown creeping stems, mostly buried

leaf.notes: small elliptic to obovate leaves, glossy dark green with an impressed net of veins, glaucous white beneath, on slender stalks

flower.form: short catkins 0.5-1.5 cm at the shoot tips after the leaves; female catkins red

fruit.form: small hairy capsules that split to release cottony seed

appearance.seasonal: deciduous; leaves yellow then drop in early autumn
appearance.silhouette: flat mat of tiny glossy leaves pressed to the gravel
appearance.refs: Flora of North America; Kew POWO

fruiting.source: Flora of North America Salix nivalis (catkins on short leafy branchlets, flowering as or after the leaves emerge; capsules); pollination by flies and bumblebees with some wind as in other arctic-alpine willows; set, timing and crop estimated

shrub.name: Mountain heath

growth.juvenile_note: A tiny seedling on moist mineral soil or moss with two minute cotyledons, then crowded, needle-like, dark green leaves. It branches from the base into a low, dense evergreen mat; stems that touch the ground root, so a patch spreads slowly where snow lies late, and after a few years it carries nodding pink bells at the shoot tips in mid-summer.
growth.source: Flora of North America Phyllodoce empetriformis (matted evergreen shrub 10-40 cm; leaves linear, 6-16 mm, grooved beneath; flowers bell-shaped, rose-pink, 5-9 mm, in terminal clusters on glandular pedicels, July-August; capsules). Germination, first flowering and age estimated.

shrub.source: Phyllodoce empetriformis, pink mountain heather: Alaska and the Yukon to California, the Rockies to Colorado; subalpine and alpine heath, snowbed margins and moist slopes; matted evergreen shrub 10-40 cm with needle-like leaves and pink bell flowers. Kew POWO; Flora of North America.

traits.native_range: subalpine and alpine heath of the western North American mountains
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

bark.notes: thin brown stems roughened by old leaf scars

leaf.notes: crowded, flat, needle-like leaves with rolled edges and a white groove beneath, spreading all round the stem like a bottlebrush

flower.form: nodding open bells 5-9 mm, rose-pink, in clusters of 5-15 at the shoot tips on long sticky stalks

fruit.form: small round brown capsules held upright

appearance.silhouette: low dense dark-green heather mat dotted with pink bells
appearance.refs: Flora of North America; Kew POWO

fruiting.source: Flora of North America (rose-pink bell flowers 5-9 mm in terminal umbel-like clusters, July-August; erect capsules); bumblebee pollination as in other Phyllodoce; set, timing and crop estimated

ground.name: Alpine sedge
ground.source: Kobresia myosuroides, dominant turf-former of dry alpine meadows in Rockies, Alps and Tibetan Plateau, 5-20 cm

traits.native_range: Kobresia myosuroides, dominant turf-former of dry alpine meadows in Rockies, Alps and Tibetan Plateau, 5-20 cm
traits.leaf_shape: narrow grass blades in a dense tussock
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are tiny tufts of thread-fine, wiry leaves that grow extremely slowly in the short, windswept alpine season. Tussocks build up over decades into dense, firm, low clumps of fine, curled leaves wrapped at the base in shiny brown old leaf sheaths, with slender 'mouse-tail' spikes held just above in early summer.
growth.source: Wikipedia (now Carex myosuroides, circumboreal mouse-tail bog sedge); timings and ages estimated from alpine sedge demography on snow-free wind-swept ridges (slow tussock growth, long-lived clumps).

ground.name: Curved sedge
ground.source: Carex curvula, dominant acid alpine grassland of the Alps/Carpathians 2000-3000 m, curved yellowish leaves

traits.native_range: Carex curvula, dominant acid alpine grassland of the Alps/Carpathians 2000-3000 m, curved yellowish leaves
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

growth.juvenile_note: A tiny tuft of thread-thin, sickle-curved leaves whose tips die back yellow-brown early, giving the curly, straw-tipped look of the adult turf. Seedlings are very rare; clones creep outward by less than 1 mm a year, so a tussock 1 m across can be around 2000 years old.
growth.source: Steinger, Korner & Schmid 1996 Oecologia 105:94 (clones of C. curvula up to ~2000 years, >7000 tillers, ~1.2 m diameter; vegetative spread <1 mm/yr); ALPANDINO course notes (seedlings rare, dense raw humus); tiller lifespan and timings estimated

ground.name: Lava moss

growth.juvenile_note: Mostly starts from broken shoot fragments (sporophytes are rare): a small tuft of wiry shoots whose narrow leaves end in long, toothed, white hair-points, so the patch looks hoary grey when dry and olive-green when wet. Shoots branch and creep outward, piling up into a springy, woolly carpet 5-15 cm deep over lava, boulders and heath; lower parts die brown.
growth.source: Wikipedia Racomitrium lanuginosum (stems to 12 cm; leaves 3-5 mm with toothed white hair-points; sporophytes rarely produced; capsules 1-1.7 mm); growth (roughly 0.5-1.5 cm of shoot a year) and carpet age estimated from bryological knowledge of Icelandic lava fields and upland heaths

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Iceland's lava fields and every cold rock; grey woolly mats that hide the ground. Kew POWO.

traits.native_range: Iceland's lava fields and every cold rock
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: thick woolly grey-white mats, leaves with long white hair-points; olive-green when wet

appearance.silhouette: grey woolly blanket over lava and rock
appearance.refs: Wikipedia, British Bryological Society field guide

ground.name: Alpine timothy

growth.juvenile_note: A loose tuft of flat, soft green leaves from short creeping bases; in its second summer it sends up slender stems topped by a short, fat, dark purple-black spike bristling with short awns.
growth.source: Flora of China / Flora Helvetica Phleum alpinum (loosely tufted, 10-50 cm; spike-like panicle ovoid to short-cylindrical, blackish-violet; wet alpine meadows); rates estimated

ground.source: Phleum alpinum L. (Kew POWO; Flora of China; Flora Helvetica): alpine timothy, loosely tufted perennial grass 10-50 cm of moist alpine meadows across the arctic-alpine northern hemisphere, including the Alps, Rockies and the Tibetan plateau (Xizang, Qinghai, 2,500-3,900 m), and down the Andes; flat leaves; dense ovoid to short-cylindrical blackish-violet spike 1-5 cm with awned glumes.

traits.native_range: arctic-alpine northern hemisphere and the Andes
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: flat soft green blades, short on the stems

flower.form: short fat blackish-violet bristly spike on a slender stem

appearance.seasonal: green in summer, straw-brown under snow
appearance.silhouette: slender stems with stubby black-purple heads

ground.silhouette: slender stems with stubby black-purple heads

ground.name: Alpine fescue

growth.juvenile_note: A seedling is a wisp of thread-fine, rolled, grey-green leaves. It tillers into a small, dense, cushion-like tuft of short bristle leaves, from which thin stems rise 5-30 cm carrying a small, narrow panicle of purple-tinged spikelets with short awns.
growth.source: Flora of North America Festuca brachyphylla (densely cespitose; culms 5-30 cm; leaves short, involute, 0.3-1 mm across; panicle 1.5-5 cm, spikelets often purplish; arctic and alpine, dry tundra, fellfield and rock). Germination, first flowering and lifespan estimated.

ground.source: Festuca brachyphylla, alpine fescue: circumpolar Arctic and the western North American mountains to Colorado and California; dry tundra, fellfield, ridges and rock ledges; a small dense tuft of bristle leaves, culms 5-30 cm. Kew POWO; Flora of North America.

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: short, thread-fine, rolled leaves, grey-green to bluish

flower.form: small narrow panicle 2-5 cm of purple-tinged, short-awned spikelets

appearance.seasonal: grey-green all summer; straw-tipped in autumn
appearance.refs: Flora of North America; Flora of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago

ground.name: Alpine moss

growth.juvenile_note: A spore lodged in a rock crack germinates into a fine green thread that buds tiny shoots. The shoots stay under 1-2 cm and pack into dense, flat, blue-green to almost black mats on bare siliceous rock, growing only fractions of a millimetre a year.
growth.source: Flora of North America Grimmia caespiticia (dense flat mats, blue-green to black-green; stems 0.5-1 cm; exposed acidic granite and quartzite at 1200-3500 m; Greenland, western North America, Eurasia). Growth rate and ages estimated from alpine Grimmia.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.source: Grimmia caespiticia (Brid.) Jur., an alpine rock moss (Mike's list spells the genus 'Gimmea'): Greenland, the western North American mountains and Eurasia including the Alps, on exposed siliceous rock above timberline; dense flat blue-green to black-green mats. Flora of North America.

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: dense flat mats of tiny lanceolate leaves with blunt hooded tips, blue-green to black-green

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; nearly black when dry, blue-green when wet
appearance.silhouette: dark blue-green moss patches on bare rock
appearance.refs: Flora of North America (Grimmia caespiticia); Greven 2003 Grimmias of the World

ground.name: Snow lichen

growth.juvenile_note: Starts from a fragment or a tiny lobe lodged among short turf on a windswept ridge, and grows into an upright tuft of flattened, wrinkled, creamy yellow-white lobes, yellower at the base, a few cm high.
growth.source: Brodo et al. Lichens of North America; Kärnefelt & Thell (Flavocetraria nivalis: fruticose, erect, 2-8 cm, pale yellowish, pitted and ridged lobes, yellow at the base; windswept alpine heaths and grassland); growth estimated

repro.note: almost never fruits; spreads by wind-blown and trampled thallus fragments

ground.source: Flavocetraria nivalis (L.) Kärnefelt & A.Thell (Index Fungorum; syn. Cetraria nivalis): snow lichen, erect fruticose lichen 2-8 cm of windswept alpine heaths, ridges and grassland in the Alps, Pyrenees, Rockies, Himalaya and the Arctic; lobes flattened, pale yellowish-white, pitted and ridged, yellow at the base.

traits.native_range: arctic tundra and wind-blown alpine ridges of the northern hemisphere
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: upright tufts of flat, crinkled, pitted creamy-yellow lobes turning yellow at the base

appearance.silhouette: creamy-white crinkled tufts on wind-blown turf
appearance.refs: Brodo et al. Lichens of North America; Wirth Flechtenflora

ground.name: Blistered rock tripe

growth.juvenile_note: A spore must meet a green alga on bare acid rock. The young thallus is a tiny dark disc pinned to the stone by a single central cord; over decades it widens into a leathery, brown-black, strongly blistered and ridged leaf 1-4 cm across, curling up at the edges when dry and going soft and olive when wet.
growth.source: Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff 2001 Lichens of North America (Umbilicaria hyperborea: umbilicate, 1-4(-6) cm, upper surface dark brown to black, strongly pustulate-ridged; on exposed acidic rock); umbilicate lichens grow fractions of a mm to ~1 mm a year in radius; ages estimated.

repro.note: a lichen: spores and fragments; no flowers

ground.source: Umbilicaria hyperborea, blistered rock tripe (the data's 'Rock tripe' is the East Asian U. esculenta): circumpolar arctic-alpine, on exposed acidic boulders and cliffs; leathery umbilicate leaves 1-4 cm, dark brown to black and blistered. Brodo et al. 2001; Index Fungorum.

traits.trunk: none — pinned to rock at one point
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

leaf.notes: leathery dark brown to black discs 1-4 cm, the upper surface blistered and ridged, edges curling when dry, pinned to the rock at the centre

appearance.seasonal: evergreen; olive-brown and limp when wet, black and brittle when dry
appearance.silhouette: dark leathery flakes scattered over boulders
appearance.refs: Brodo et al. 2001 Lichens of North America; Funga Nordica lichen keys

ground.name: Tundra puffball

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through the soil or litter; 'wind' = spores.

ground.source: Lycoperdon cretaceum Berk. (syn. Calvatia cretacea), arctic puffball: circumpolar arctic-alpine, most frequent in the Arctic with scattered records in the Alps and Rockies; small chalk-white puffballs on bare soil, among moss and dwarf shrubs in tundra and fellfield. Index Fungorum; Larsson & Jeppson 2008; IUCN Red List (Lycoperdon cretaceum).

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

cap.form: small round to pear-shaped puffball 1-4 cm with a short pinched base, no cap or gills
cap.notes: chalk-white outer skin of tiny pointed warts that rub off; ages grey-brown, opens by a pore at the top and puffs olive-brown spores

appearance.habit: single or scattered on bare soil, among moss and dwarf shrubs
appearance.seasonal: fruits in late summer; the papery case lingers into winter
appearance.silhouette: small chalk-white balls on the tundra floor
appearance.refs: Index Fungorum; Larsson & Jeppson 2008 (Lycoperdaceae); Funga Nordica
